set.overview: A long-standing classic on the rightmost, third buttress of Hallett Peak above Emerald Lake in Rocky Mountain National Park, about 900 feet and eight pitches of trad climbing. A rockfall in 1999 stripped the original first two pitches, so the start now goes through the scar at a runout 5.10 or begins on the neighbouring line to the right at 5.8 or 5.9. It is busy and popular, but the dihedral on pitch three is smaller than it looks and wayfinding trouble keeps many parties from getting past the lower pitches.
hazards: Loose, fractured rock in the 1999 rockfall scar and on the first pitches, where the start is runout
Loose rock where the line crosses between the second and third buttresses
The pitch three dihedral is easy to misread, and it is easy to wander off route there
Afternoon thunderstorms and hail have caught parties on the descent after a late-morning top-out
Loose gully on the way down, so stay clear of anyone above

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: no page gave a figure for this line. Season skipped: only raptor closure dates and one August snow note, no stated window.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead and follow the trail past Alberta Falls, The Loch and Lake of Glass to Sky Pond, a little over four miles with roughly 2,000 feet of climbing, taking about two hours. Leave the trail near Sky Pond, cross the talus field toward the spires and scramble up to the foot of the south face, about 15 minutes more. Snow can linger on this approach in early summer and be icy at dawn, so carry traction.
hazards: Icy snow patches on the approach in early summer and early morning
Queues and long waits at the rappel stations on this very popular route
The fifth of six rappels uses nearly all of a 60 m rope, which is tight for a light climber
Marmots near the base chew and carry off gear left unattended

evidence.fact: about 4.5 miles from Glacier Gorge trailhead to the Petit Grepon area, one way
4.2 mi trail to Sky Pond and beyond, 2,040 ft ascent; base is about 15 min past Sky Pond

review.notes: dist_km is trailhead to base of the climb (the walk-in), 4.5 mi; the two pages end at slightly different points. Gain skipped: only a figure to Sky Pond (2,040 ft) and an unopened 2,700 ft round-trip snippet. Season skipped: no stated window.

hazards: Rotten rock and rockfall in North Chimney and on Broadway, the access to the wall
Drips from the ice plug can soak the belay at Table Ledge
The 5.10c pitch below Table Ledge is crumbly
The last 5.8 pitch can be wet, icy and runout
The bolts at the bivy ledge need replacing

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: no opened page gave a trailhead-to-top figure for D1 (only to Chasm Lake, 4.2 mi / about 2,400 ft already in the approach), and the only season note is that June is often dry.

set.approach: Park at the primitive campground on Castle Valley road, a quarter to half mile past the cattle guard on the left. Hike up the wash following cairns to a dirt road, cross it at the cairn and signpost, and continue on the trail toward the tower. The climb up to the base is steep and takes about an hour for a fit party; it finishes with a short fourth class step and a ledge that circles round to the south side.
hazards: Wet sandstone is fragile, so stay off after rain
Summer heat can approach 100 F with no shade on the sunny south side
Calcite-crusted offwidth crux on the third pitch with a bolt that is poor
Stuck ropes on the rappels and other parties crowding the line, especially in spring and fall

evidence.fact: approach hike 2.2 km one way (listing 4.31 km, likely round trip)
4.2 km out and back, so about 2.1 km one way

review.notes: Gain and distance are to the base of the tower (the whole walk-in). The 10adventures gain may count descents too, so it could be a little high. Season skipped: pages say only that spring and fall are busy and summer is hot.

set.overview: A pioneering desert aid classic on the Titan in the Fisher Towers, working crack lines up the east side and the north ridge to the detached spire called the Finger, with an exposed traverse beneath it. It is eight aid pitches plus a fourth class scramble to the summit, mostly clean aid with a roof on the fourth pitch and long reaches on the last. Expect plenty of old fixed gear, a bivy ledge near The Duck, and a long day or two days on the wall.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the top of pitch eight to the top of pitch seven, then to the anchor by The Duck on pitch six. From there, make more rappels with two ropes down the gully to the base. As an alternative, two double-rope rappels down the cliff to the west near the base save the walk back around the tower. Jugging the descent line is slow and unpleasant, so move fast.
hazards: Moab sandstone is fragile when wet, so stay off during and for days after rain
Dirty, mank-covered cracks and loose rock in places
Old or doubtful fixed gear, including a poor star drive on pitch four and fixed tricams
Bolts eroded by mud in places, and dicey gear at some belays
Sudden violent storms and a long exposed roof at the end of pitch eight

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: a walk-in around the tower with no stated figure. Rappel count after pitch six not stated (single source, search snippets only), so I left it uncounted.

set.overview: A long, wandering Yosemite Valley classic of about 2,000 feet and 16 pitches up a band of low-angle granite on the north side of the valley. Pitches range from fourth class scrambling to sustained cracks, with a chimney start, an offwidth, a pendulum on pitch nine, and a slick slab exit on the last pitch. Most parties climb it at 5.7 with one point of aid off a fixed line, and it frees at 5.10-; it often links with routes on North Dome.
set.approach: Park at the Church Bowl picnic area (free) or the Ahwahnee lot and pick up the well-trodden trail that carries a carabiner sign. The walk to the base is short, roughly ten minutes. Stay well right of Serenity Crack; the climb begins in a chimney at the back of a large left-facing corner.
set.descent_text: Two ways down. The traditional way is to hike over the top of Washington Column and descend North Dome Gully, which is sandy and exposed and easy to lose in the dark. The faster alternative is the rappel route, about ten rappels with a single 60 m rope, though some stations are hard to find. Allow one to three hours for the raps and avoid starting the gully at night.
hazards: A loose block on the belay ledge at the top of pitches seven and eight, and loose blocks left of the traverse
Old, degrading rappel anchors and a worn fixed line at the pendulum
Polished slab on the last pitch with thin protection and one very old bolt
The walk-off and the rappels are hard to follow in the dark, so start early
Full sun by late morning, and slow parties with few places to pass

review.notes: Season skipped: spring is wet and summer hot per comments, but no window is stated. Ten-rappel count agrees across two pages that may share a topo.

set.overview: A famous Yosemite spire climb known more for its position and novelty than for hard climbing: two pitches, about 250 feet, graded 5.7 C2. The first pitch follows pin scars and fixed gear to a grainy flaring offwidth and a ledge; the second traverses left, then a bolt ladder and low-angle slab reach the top. Access is from the rim, by rappel into the notch, and most parties return to the rim by a Tyrolean traverse, so rigging matters more than the climbing.
set.approach: Reach the rim by hiking from the Upper Yosemite Falls trail near Camp 4, or from the Tioga Road side, to the Yosemite Point area. Plan on roughly two to three and a half hours of hiking, so start early. From trees and bolts near Yosemite Point, rappel into the notch below the spire to reach the start of the climb.
set.descent_text: Return to the rim by the Tyrolean traverse from the top of the spire to the rim anchors, then jug back up as needed. Alternatively, rappel back into the notch. Take care that the rope knot does not catch on a flake when pulling.
hazards: Serious exposure on the spire and on the Tyrolean traverse
Rope drag and tangles, especially on the second pitch and while rigging the Tyrolean
Some fixed gear is old or doubtful, so test before trusting it
A cold, windy notch where a stormy night has caught a party

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: approach time is only roughly given, and falcon closures are a restriction not a window.

set.overview: A long, wide and physical Yosemite Valley classic up the north face of Sentinel Rock: 14 pitches of cracks, chimneys and squeezes, at 5.10- by the old rating and 5.10b by the newer one. The 5.8 and 5.9 offwidth pitches are the real test, with the Wilson Overhang at 5.10a, a 5.10b corner and flare, and the exposed Narrows squeeze. Plan on a full day, with a descent gully that is no easier than the climb.
set.approach: Park at the Four Mile trailhead and follow the trail a long half mile to a narrow talus slope that leads into the trees; it may be marked by a cairn. If you miss it, continue east to a streambed and backtrack. Follow the climbers' trail up the talus to the base of the rock, at a steep wide west-trending ramp whose catwalk ledges are third and fourth class and gain about a third of the height.
set.descent_text: Head east through manzanita and boulders into a steep, loose gully and follow the trail on its south wall, rappelling or making a fourth to low fifth class bypass. Cross the spring-fed stream, then head north across steep slabs, staying mid-slab or on the west half, and bushwhack to the climbers' trail. Do not start the upper part of this descent in the dark.
hazards: Loose, steep descent gully and bushwhacking, with serious falls and rockfall there
Strenuous, exposed offwidth and chimney pitches, including the Narrows
Darkness on the descent, which turns into risky downclimbing or extra rappels
Falcon closures in spring, and fire or smoke closures

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: no figure or window stated on any page I opened.

set.approach: Park at a pullout on the valley loop road past Bridalveil Falls and find the climbers' trail. The approach is short and straightforward but steep, climbing about 800 feet to the base of the buttress.
set.descent_text: Two options. The rappel line is a dedicated route just left of the tenth belay, using a 60 m rope for short rappels of about 20 m; do not climb the eleventh pitch. The walk-off follows a cairned bootpath and the faint Kat Walk to the gully between Middle and Upper Cathedral, which needs several rappels or scrambling and is hard to follow in the dark.
hazards: Snow in the descent gully early in the season can make it the crux
Exposed third class slabs and ledges on the walk-off, with a steep drop at the gully end
Rappel anchors in the gully damaged by rockfall
Falcon closures in spring, and fire or smoke closures

review.notes: Gain skipped: only the 800 ft approach climb, not a summit gain. Distance and season not stated. Page numbering of pitches is inconsistent (9 vs 10/11).

set.overview: The classic big wall on Half Dome, 23 pitches graded 5.9 with a little aid, climbed in a long day or with a bivouac. It is one of the most popular routes on the dome and finishes by walking off the top via the cable route.
set.approach: Two ways from Happy Isles. The standard approach hikes the Mist Trail through Little Yosemite Valley, about eight miles to the shoulder of Half Dome, then descends along the face to the start. The faster option goes past Mirror Lake and up the slabs, but needs skilled route finding, very steep hiking and fixed lines.
hazards: The slab approach by Mirror Lake has steep route finding and fixed lines
Closure for nesting falcons in spring, and for fire or smoke
Long exposed day with an afternoon descent down the cables

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: 8 mi to the shoulder is single-source and not the wall start; a 4,800 ft figure appeared only in unopened search snippets. The 2015 rockfall note came from a search summary of Wikipedia, which I did not open: drop it if the lead cannot confirm.

set.overview: The most famous big wall in Yosemite, about 3,000 feet and 31 pitches up the middle of the southwest face of El Capitan. At 5.9 C2 it is the easiest full-length route on the wall, which is why it draws so many parties, but it is sustained and exposed. Much of the climbing is 5.10 or easier and many people climb it in four or five days.
set.approach: From El Capitan Meadow, cross the road and take one of the obvious trails to a clearing. Follow the worn path north and slightly west to the wall, then go up and left around its foot and traverse back right to a dirt ledge at the start of the first pitch. It takes only 10 to 15 minutes.
set.descent_text: The standard way down from the summit is the East Ledges, a mix of rappelling, downclimbing and talus scrambling that has caused injuries and a fatality; consider waiting for morning light. On the route itself you can rappel from any pitch, but route finding matters and parties have got lost on the standard rap line.
hazards: Leader falls from pulled gear are the most common incident
Weather and stranding during the four to five days most parties spend on the wall
Falling objects, rope-cutting rockfall, pendulums and rappel errors
Runoff above the upper camps after rain or snowmelt
East Ledges descent, which has caused injuries

review.notes: Season skipped: fall and winter are popular but no window is stated.

set.overview: A very long El Capitan route, 35 pitches and about 3,500 feet, possibly the longest on the wall. The first ten pitches, the Free Blast, are low-angle and mostly free at 5.10, then the wall steepens into aid, a finger crack on the headwall and a roof taken on mostly fixed gear. There are many ledges, including a flat bivy on El Cap Spire. The route has little fixed gear and many spots without fixed anchors.
set.approach: Follow the El Capitan trail to the base of the Nose, then head uphill and left a short way to the foot of the route. It starts with easy climbing to a ledge and then a finger crack above.
set.descent_text: From the top, a few fixed lines return climbers to the ground. Some parties rappel about 200 feet from the top of the Mammoth Terraces to Heart Ledges to bail from the upper wall.
hazards: Hollow Flake pitch needs a big pendulum and is very runout above
The Ear bombay chimney, which narrows as you climb
The Sewer almost always seeps water and has a hanging belay
Little fixed gear and some belays without fixed anchors
Crowds on the Free Blast pitches

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: no figures, and only a falcon closure is stated. Fixed-line count left uncounted (one page says four, a snippet said three).
